headlines.title: San Jose mayor meets with neighbors complaining about data center noise
headlines.description: On Wednesday night, Mayor Matt Mahan met with some South San Jose residents who say they’ve been dealing with a low, constant hum and bright lights shinning into their backyards coming from data centers nearby. Neighbors said the noise can get even louder when temperatures rise. Their concerns come as San Jose looks at whether its rules for data centers need to be strengthened. Denisa and Jay Filichia live in South San Jose. Their backyard faces several data centers along Great Oaks Boulevard, separated by a few roads and train tracks. “We’re not anti-data center at all, it’s more the noise and the lights that are bothering us,” Filichia said. Denisa has been in contact with the city, and on Wednesday night, Mayor Matt Mahan went to the neighborhood to hear the noise for himself. The mayor and the neighbors then walked toward Monterey Road, getting closer to the data centers. The neighbors’ complaints come as data centers themselves are facing increased scrutiny in other cities as these facilities usually require significant amounts of electricity and water, causing a lot of anger in some communities. Some are even imposing temporary moratoriums on new data centers, all together. San Jose hasn’t. The city is hearing from residents and considering stronger standards. “We should require that if a data center in San Jose can access our purple pipe, that’s our recycled water network, that they need to hook up to that system and become a customer and pay for that water,” Mahan said. Mahan says that would also help the city expand its recycled water system. And for Denisa and Jay, he says he’ll work with the data centers to try to address the noise and light. “We’ll talk to them. Maybe they can put some insulation or shielding around the fans and quiet down on their end. maybe we can turn down the lights,” Mahan said. San Jose plans to hold a series of town halls in the coming months as it works on potential new standards and regulations for those data centers. As for any proposed rules they come up with, they’re expected to come before the San Jose City Council in December.

headlines.title: Councilwoman receives death threats and assaulted over Pittsburg data center
headlines.description: A Pittsburg councilwoman says she’s gotten death threats and was recently assaulted over the city’s approved data center. “When they become threatening to us. When they become violent. I say that because I was assaulted,” Councilmember Arlene Kobata said on a podcast. Kobata said the woman, angry over the city approving a data center, assaulted her at a public event. “She grabbed me and shoved me a couple of times, and had some strong words with me,” she said. Kobata says that’s not the only scary incident she’s experienced as the community has become increasingly fired up over the 77-acre data center set to be built on the former site of a golf course. She says she and others have received harassing emails and even death threats. Kobata was a member of the planning commission who agreed the project is compliant with California environmental regulations. She insists the center will not be a drain on natural resources. The threats are drawing criticism from many in the community, includingPittsburg’smayor, who points out the city has paused further action while it conducts community outreach. In a statement, Mayor Dionne Adams said, “Violence against anyone is never the answer. We can disagree passionately, but we must do so peacefully and ensure every resident has a safe and meaningful opportunity to be heard.” Kobata insists the data center will not harm the community and says she was not on council when it was approved. She also says she won’t let the threats silence her. “We’re tough we’re still gonna stand tough for what we believe is right for the residents,” she said.

headlines.title: Brentwood community mourns Liberty High School students killed in crash
headlines.description: The Liberty High School community in Brentwood gathered on Thursday to remember two students killed in a crash over the weekend. Caden Kyle and Dominic Ferrari were killed in a crash near Deer Valley and Balfour roads just after midnight Sunday A third Liberty High School student remains hospitalized in critical condition. The school’s principal Efa Huckaby says even those who didn’t know the students personally were feeling the pain. “A lot of the community, even if they didn’t know the young people, they’re still affected because it’s one of our own here,” he said. For some, the connection to Kyle and Ferrari goes back years, including friends who have known them since elementary school. The principal says bringing the school community together was important, to give students and families a place to grieve and lean on each other. “We like to think of Liberty High School as the center of the community, and so to be able to open our facilities for the families and for the students to have a space to grieve,” Huckaby said. Antioch police are leading the investigation into the crash. Investigators are asking anyone who may have witnessed what happened or has surveillance or dashcam video to come forward.

headlines.title: ‘We want answers': Family of Nvidia researcher continues to question suicide ruling
headlines.description: The family of a 32-year-old Nvidia researcher who died in July is calling on Palo Alto police to continue to dig into the circumstances of his death, which authorities have ruled a suicide. Irfan Al-Hussaini was found unresponsive in his Palo Alto home on July 22 and died about a week later. His family is urging state and local authorities to look further into his death, saying the circumstances surrounding his passing are suspicious. “The brother I knew would never, ever take his own life,” Irfan’s sister, Sarah Al-Hussaini, said Thursday during a news conference in front of Palo Alto City Hall. Irfan was a senior AI researcher at Nvidia who had recently been promoted and was focused on his promising future. While authorities ruled his death a suicide, his family argues the evidence they have says otherwise. “What little information we were told does not match with the information we have gathered so far and the things we know,” Sarah said. The family said Irfan presented research to about 15 colleagues until about 9 a.m. on July 22. At 10:02 a.m., a Slack message was sent from his account to his manager saying his wife was not feeling well and would take the day off, the family said. A 911 call was placed about 20 minutes later. Doctors told the family initial scans suggested Irfan had been without oxygen for nearly 30 to 60 minutes. “So who sent that 10:02 text?” Sarah said. “Does that text fit with the medical timeline?” The family and their attorney, Tony Brass, said there was no suicide note left. They also question whether domestic violence was overlooked. “The plan that they’re supposed to accept is that he hung himself from a door while his wife was home and he did it in a way that she did not detect or know that that was happening,” Brass said. “That makes no sense.” The family said Irfan was wearing an Oura ring that morning and believes its data could potentially help establish a timeline for investigators. “We want a proper investigation, we want answers, we want justice for Irfan,” Sarah said. Palo Alto police said the case remains under investigation, pending the medical examiner’s report. The department said it has received materials from the family and others, adding that neither police nor the medical examiner have identified evidence of foul play. An attorney for Irfan’s widow said she fully cooperated with the investigation and that a full forensic autopsy was performed on Aug. 31. The attorney said Irfan’s widow has no objections to forensic materials being reviewed. If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or chat live at 988lifeline.org. You can also visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional support.

headlines.title: Berkeley's Triple Rock Brewery to close after 40 years in downtown
headlines.description: A beloved brewery in downtown Berkeley has announced that it is planning to close after four decades of operations. Triple Rock Brewery and Taphouse on Shattuck Avenue will close by the end of the year, its owners wrote in a post on the brewery’s website. The business opened in 1986, originally called Roaring Rock Brewery. The owners, brothers John and Martin Reid, say this is the oldest, continuously operating brewpub in the U.S. In the post on the website, the owners said they are ready to retire. The owners told SF Gate that the general decline in alcohol sales also contributed to their decision to close. The brewpub will remain open until the end of the Cal Berkeley semester in December, patrons are encouraged to come by and share memories before this chapter closes.

headlines.title: Morgan Hill winery struggles amid low demand and bug concerns
headlines.description: A Morgan Hill winery is struggling as trade pressures, weather concerns and lower demand plague the state’s vineyard business. Guglielmo Winery has been serving the Morgan Hill community since 1925, after George Guglielmo’s grandfather bought the land that same year. However, the winery has been struggling due to several concerns, including lower demand as young people don’t drink as much as the previous generations did. The glassy winged sharpshooter, an invasive insect that can kill crops, is another concern at the business. Santa Clara County’s Division of Agriculture says it’s done going door to door, searching for plants that may be harboring the pest, but are still looking for grapevine plants sold earlier this year at Costco. Other issues affecting the business also include trade pressures and weather concerns.

headlines.title: San Francisco Opera and orchestra musicians reach tentative agreement
headlines.description: The San Francisco Opera announced on Thursday it has reached a tentative agreement with the orchestra musicians for a new four-year contract to end the strike. The agreement spans from Aug. 1 through July 31, 2030, and is still subject to ratification, according to San Francisco Opera. The company added its 104th season will open on Sept. 22 with Giuseppe Verdi’s Simon Boccanegra. Despite reaching an agreement, the Opera noted weekend performances will remain canceled, saying “staging world-class opera performances requires significant rehearsal, preparation and planning”. Those with tickets can choose their options by visiting the Opera’s website. The strike was announced Saturday afternoon, prompting the cancelation of the Opera’s 104th season opening night and many other performances. Musicians said over the weekend they had been in negotiation with the Opera right up until Saturday’s scheduled opening night performance but could not reach an agreement. “I am deeply grateful that we have reached a tentative agreement on a new contract, one that addresses important structural changes while providing a fair agreement for our Musicians,” San Francisco Opera General Director Matthew Shilvock said. “I want to thank both negotiating committees and recognize the leadership of Mayor Lurie, Matthew Goudeau and the mediators. All have worked tirelessly over the past week to realize this agreement. We look forward to welcoming our talented company members and guest artists, as well as our cherished patrons and donors, back to the theater. Most of all, we look forward to coming together again and reconnecting through the collective beauty of the arts.” “We are heartened to have reached a tentative deal that provides a fair contract and stability for the members of the orchestra,” San Francisco Opera Orchestra Associate Principal Oboist and Chair of the Orchestra Negotiating Committee Gabe Young said. “We are grateful to Mayor Lurie and his team, who put in long hours over the past several days to help broker this agreement, and we want to thank the public and Opera patrons for their patience and support through what has been a challenging process for our musicians. We look forward to working together to build on the progress being made at the San Francisco Opera, and we cannot wait to return to the pit to begin this new season and perform once again for the company we love.” To learn more about the Opera’s season, visit its website.

headlines.title: Pop-up restaurant in San Francisco seeks new home after rent triples
headlines.description: A San Francisco restaurant that started as a pop-up is looking for a new home after the owner said he recently learned the rent for his space would triple to about $25,000. Al Pastor Papi owner and chef Miguel Escobedo opened the pop-up in July 2025 with the help of the Vacant to Vibrant program, which helped him find a restaurant-ready location. “They were hoping to find a strong local brand that could probably make some noise here,” Escobedo said. “We were connected and Al Pastor Papi pop-up was born.” Escobedo said it has been a fun adventure. The agreement was to do a pop-up for a year and a half through the end of 2026. Then the hope was to work out a deal to stay on a more long-term basis. “The typical agreement with Vacant to Vibrant is 10% of what you sell, which is amazing, unheard of,” Escobedo said. Escobedo said they worked out a deal with the landlord and the future looked bright. But now there are new owners and the asking price of rent changed dramatically. “Pretty much tripled with what the new landlord was wanting from us and in fact offered us, but I couldn’t accept it,” Escobedo said. NBC Bay Area reached out to the management company but didn’t immediately hear back. Escobedo said the Vacant to Vibrant program has been very supportive all along. In a statement, the executive director of SF New Deal, which runs the program, said their team works closely with every program participant to help them navigate both their pop-up term and what comes next, saying, “Miguel and the team at Al Pastor Papi have brought an inspiring concept downtown through their pop-up and we have been actively working with them to explore opportunities and determine the best path forward beyond their current term.” In the meantime, Escobedo plans to keep serving his customers while he figures out what the next chapter looks like. “Just try to find another home for Al Pastor Papi,” he said. “I want this for my family and I want this for my community.”

headlines.title: Deputies help rescue abandoned dogs in Vallejo
headlines.description: Solano County deputies helped rescue four dogs abandoned in Vallejo on Monday. Deputies say someone dumped the animals near Lake Herman Road. A Good Samaritan helped deputies corral two puppies. They found another pup nearby and the momma dog in a ravine. All four dogs were taken to a shelter and are now looking for their forever homes.

headlines.title: Fundraiser campaign aims to bring air conditioning to Oakland Unified schools
headlines.description: A parent-led fundraising campaign is underway to raise tens of thousands of dollars for air conditioning in Oakland Unified schools. The goal is to raise $100,000 to cool 200 classrooms across the school district and prevent conditions such as temperatures topping 90 degrees inside schools like Manzanita Community Elementary. “It’s really important that our kids have safe places that they can go to, and if it is hot and if it is over 90 degrees in their classroom, that is not safe,” Co-founder of Cooling the Schools Alison Mata said. Last march, the parents raised $6,000 for AC units at Sequoia Elementary. Now, they want to cool classrooms districtwide, prioritizing the hottest classrooms at Title 1 schools and those with the least fundraising capacity. A donor is already promising to match the first $5,000 raised. The group is working with the district, but feels it can get the cool air moving faster. “Let’s get these in the classrooms. We are in September, October and these can be the hottest months that we have so it’s important that we are not waiting until the next year, the year after,” Mata said. Students at United Success Academy say they can feel the heat, especially during days like last week when temperatures hit the high 90s. “Our schools were not built for hot climate and so we are trying to address it, and it will take about a decade to address all the issues across the schools,” OUSD Chief System and Service Officer Facilities and Operations Preston Thomas said. With 2,100 classrooms without ventilation or cooling, the district says it’s a massive fix. Over the next two years, it plans to use part of $12 million in bond funding to target the hottest schools with window film, cool roof systems, better ventilation and “living school yards,” reducing asphalt. Five schools are also getting major cooling upgrades, but the district estimates it needs up to $1 billion to address heat across all its schools making community partnerships even more important. “There are going to be areas where we don’t have resources and funding and they are really taking an equity frame to try to utilize some of the data and partnership with the district to try to address things we might not be able to reach right now,” Thomas said.

headlines.title: California gas prices jump to over $6 a gallon on average
headlines.description: The average price for a gallon of gas in California jumped 19 cents in the past week to $6.08. In San Francisco, the average gallon costs $6.23. In Oakland, it’s up to $6.13. In San Jose, the average is now $6.07. The national average is up more than $1 a gallon compared to a year ago. The war with Iran and uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz continue to be the main reasons for climbing prices.

headlines.title: BART reports major delays due to equipment problem in San Francisco
headlines.description: BART reported major delays Thursday afternoon due to an equipment problem on the track at the 24th St. Mission station in San Francisco. Muni was offering service between the Daly City and Embarcadero stations in the meantime, BART said. Additional information wasn’t immediately available. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. This story uses functionality that may not work in our app. Click here to open the story in your web browser.
